title: fix: preserve existing indentation when enabling plugins (bug #8)
body:
## Bug #8: `enable_plugins` silently drops every already-enabled plugin

`enable_plugins` hardcoded a two-space indent for both the `enabled:` key and its list items.

On a config that uses four-space list items — which is what Hermes itself writes — inserting `  - name` immediately before an existing `    - other` makes YAML parse the second line as a continuation of the first string:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
  - hermes-handoff      # inserted, 2 spaces
  - hermes-jev          # inserted, 2 spaces
    - agentmemory       # pre-existing, 4 spaces -> now part of the line above
    - dynamic-workflows
```

The two pre-existing plugins are silently absorbed. Exit code is 0 and nothing is printed, so the failure is invisible until something that depends on those plugins stops working.

**Fix:** detect the indentation of the existing key line and of the first list item, and match both. Falls back to the previous two-space behaviour when the block is empty.

## Second path to the same failure (found while fixing the above)

A flow-style list never matched the key regex at all:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled: ['agentmemory', 'dynamic-workflows']
```

`key` came back `None`, so the code took the insert branch, added a *second* `enabled:` key, and the new entries were silently ignored (`['agentmemory', 'dynamic-workflows']` won).

Flow-style is now normalised into a block list — preserving the existing entries — before the shared logic runs.

## Verification

Six cases, all passing:

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| A: four-space items (the #8 report) | pre-existing plugin absorbed | preserved, indent matched |
| B: Hermes default shape | same as A | preserved |
| C: flow-style list | duplicate key, new entries lost | normalised, all entries kept |
| D: `enabled: []` | ok | ok |
| E: no `plugins:` section | ok | ok |
| F: run twice (idempotent) | ok | ok, file unchanged |

Tested against a real Hermes install: installing this repo's two plugins on a machine whose `plugins.enabled` held `agentmemory` and `dynamic-workflows` left both intact.

## Also

Adds the missing `jev_search` entry to `hermes/plugin/hermes-jev/plugin.yaml` — the plugin registers six tools but declared five, so `hermes plugins validate` reported an undeclared tool.

title: install: write plugin names at the indent the list already uses
body:
## What was reported

On a live install, `install.py` added its two plugin names to `plugins.enabled` and switched six
plugins off. `yaml.safe_load` had no complaint:

```python
enabled == ["hermes-handoff",
            "hermes-jev - a2a-platform - basic - browser-firecrawl - drain - openai-codex - openrouter"]
```

## Why

The config already indented that list four spaces in:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
    - a2a-platform
    - basic
    ...
```

`enable_plugins` wrote every name it added at two spaces — `["  - " + name]`, hardcoded — which
is the same column as the item above it, not a new item. Both shapes are valid YAML, so nothing
objected: six plugins were folded into one scalar and the next gateway restart read the list as
two plugins. It was repaired by hand on the machine that found it.

The same line has a second half: a list written at two spaces in is just as valid, and a fix that
hardcodes four breaks that config instead.

## The change

The column now comes from the file. `enable_plugins` reads the indent of the `enabled:` key, reads
the indent of the first `- ` item under it, and writes its own lines at those columns. Four spaces
in stays four, two stays two. A `plugins:` section with no `enabled:` key gets one beside the keys
it does have. Nothing else about the text edit changed: comments, ordering and other settings
survive, removal restores the file byte for byte, and the backup behaviour is untouched.

## The test

`tests/test_install.py` gained `PluginsListIndentTests`. A text assertion cannot see this bug —
the old output is a well-formed file that reads back wrong — so each case edits the config and
then reads it with `yaml.safe_load`:

- six names already there four spaces in, plus the two this repo ships, must come back as **8
  separate names**, none containing ` - `;
- the same with the list two spaces in;
- `plugins:` with no `enabled:` key, and no `plugins:` section at all.

The four-space case fails on `main` with the folded string from the report and passes after the
change; the other three are there so an over-correcting fix cannot pass. PyYAML moved ahead of the
suite in `.github/workflows/test.yml` so that test cannot silently skip in CI.

## Verification

- `python -m unittest discover -s tests` — 850 tests. The 33 pre-existing failures and errors are
  Windows-only (symlink privilege, POSIX paths, `/bin/sh`), unchanged from `main`; no new failures,
  and every `test_install` config test passes.
- `python scripts/check_release.py` — clean.
- A simulation of the reported config: 8 plugins before and after, `any(" - " in n)` false,
  `--uninstall` restores the file byte for byte.

CI is Ubuntu and macOS, where the whole suite is expected green.

title: Linux: read the window, then read the controls (AT-SPI roles, cua-driver text replies, keystore)
body:
Linux: read the window, then read the controls (AT-SPI roles, cua-driver text replies, keystore)

Three ways the runner was macOS-only, each found by running it on Linux against cua-driver
0.23.x and watching the loop do nothing.

1. `INTERACTIVE_ROLES` held only the macOS spellings. AT-SPI reports bare lower case —
   `push button`, `entry`, `check box`, `page tab` — and offers no `AXPress` action, so
   `element_rows` filtered out every control: a window whose tree held 35 labelled controls
   came back as "no interactive elements observed" and the loop could not move. The
   lower-case names are added; a role that is not a control (`label`, `panel`, `filler`,
   `separator`, `frame`) is still dropped, because a click on one is a candidate spent on
   nothing and the chooser contract holds 32.

2. `observe` read only `result.structuredContent`. cua-driver 0.23.x answers
   `get_window_state` with `content[0].text`, the same state as a JSON string, and no
   `structuredContent`, so every observation returned `{}` on a window it could see.
   Structured content still wins where it exists; a text part that is not JSON is not an
   answer, it falls through to the empty state as before.

3. The credential step called macOS `security` unconditionally. On Linux that raises
   `FileNotFoundError` from `subprocess.run` and killed the run a dozen lines before
   `jevkit.keystore` — which already resolves environment → OS secret store → credentials
   file — could be consulted. The `security` path is now taken only where `security` exists,
   and `openrouter` the same way.

Tests: `LinuxTreeTests` (lower-case roles offered, non-control roles still dropped) and
`DriverReplyShapeTests` (the text reply parsed, structured content still winning, junk text
not treated as an answer). `tests/test_gui_agent.py`: 78 tests, green.

title: docs: verify an agent's own answers before they ship (output guardrails pattern)
body:
New pattern page under docs/: using Jev to judge the agent's own outgoing reply **before delivery**, against the context that produced it.

## What it adds

- **Two Noul questions, one call**: `contradicts_context` (invented facts / contradictions vs the context) + `leaks_secrets` (credentials in the reply).
- **Measured on a live Hermes setup** (16 labelled cases, 2 rounds): wrong date → 0.97, invented model name → 0.96, clean reply → 0.16, GPG passphrase leak → 0.80, private LAN IP → 0.09 (no false alarm). ~$0.00002 per reply, ~600ms.
- **The one rule that makes it work**: the context must travel in the state. Without it, the same invented fact scores 0.48 (coin flip); with it, 0.96. This differs from routing/triage gates where the state is a short record — here the gate is only as honest as the evidence passed.
- Same three-way mode switch (off/shadow/on), same fail-open contract; the gate **holds** and explains, never rewrites (re-drafting is frontier-model work).
- Privacy posture matching memory: capped reply (600 chars) / context (500 chars); a reply containing a credential is the reply the gate exists to flag, and the agent re-drafts without it.

## Why this pattern

The repo's docs cover judging the *inputs* of a run (skills, results, turns). This page documents judging the *output* — the other side of the same contract: code owns control flow, Jev owns the judgment calls, and the answer that ships is the one Jev would not flag.

Follows the house rules from CONTRIBUTING.md and the fleet doc: shadow-before-steer, fail-open, Jev never writes.

Refs: docs/wiring-triage-into-a-live-pipeline.md (adapter discipline), docs/mailbox-sorting.md (threshold constants style).

title: Honour TYPESAFE_BASE_URL so the skills can run against a local Jev-compatible endpoint
body:
`jevkit/client.py:23` pins `ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"`, and `_http_transport` (line 236) defaults to it. The official TypeSafe SDKs read `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` for exactly this, so honouring it here would let the skills run against any Jev-compatible endpoint without a code change: a corporate proxy, a mock in tests, or a local server.

Suggested change, three lines:

```python
BASE_URL = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_BASE_URL", "https://api.typesafe.ai").rstrip("/")
ENDPOINT = f"{BASE_URL}/v1/systemone"
```

with the key check relaxed when the base URL is not the TypeSafe host (a local server ignores the bearer token), the same way the `openrouter` transport already carries its own key logic.

I verified the request and answer shapes the client sends against two local servers: [stuntd](https://github.com/bladedevoff/stuntd) (Laya behind the Jev API, `http://127.0.0.1:8787`, which also records the answers and trains a head per question) and laya-server. Both accept the body `ask()` builds and return `answers` in the shape the parser expects, including `probabilities` and `x-typesafe-request-id`. Happy to send the PR if you prefer that over the issue.

title: routing: reuse the difficulty answer to set reasoning effort
body:
A turn already pays one Jev call to find out how hard it is. This PR spends that same answer a second time — to pick the **reasoning-effort level** for the request — so an easy turn stops burning a frontier model's full thinking budget, and a hard one is not starved of it.

## How it works

- `route.decide` now carries the raw Jev answers back on the decision (a kept turn included — a kept turn still paid for the judgement), so the effort pick needs **no second Jev call**.
- New `jevkit/effort.py` maps the difficulty score (0–3) onto a level table. Default: `low / medium / high / xhigh`; configurable via `{"effort": {"enabled": true, "levels": [...]}}` in `routing.json`.
- The plugin stamps the picked level onto the outgoing request in both spellings: top-level `reasoning_effort` and `extra_body.reasoning.effort`. A manual `/effort` override set by the user still wins (it rides on the same fields).
- Works whether routing is `on`, `shadow`, or `off` — the model swap still obeys the mode; the effort pick applies to whichever model the turn ends up on. Each pick is logged (`"kind": "effort"`) to `jev-decisions.jsonl`, so a day in shadow shows where real turns land before committing.

## Fail-open, as required

- Off by default: no `effort` block in `routing.json` → nothing changes.
- Jev down, slow, or a malformed/missing score → the request goes out exactly as it would have without the plugin.
- Malformed level tables are refused (empty, >8 levels, bad type) rather than guessed at.
- Privacy boundary unchanged: nothing new is sent to Jev — this only *reads* an answer routing already bought.

## Tests

- `tests/test_effort.py` (new, 17 tests): bucket edges, invalid/missing scores, spread-vs-score precedence, disabled/malformed/absent config, custom tables.
- `tests/test_plugin_middleware.py` (+5): effort applied on a routed swap, applied when the model stays, not applied when disabled, custom table honored end-to-end, malformed table fails open, shadow mode applies effort without swapping the model.
- Full suite: 955 tests OK locally; `scripts/check_release.py` clean.

title: Routing silently no-ops when the Hermes provider name is not a models.dev provider id (custom -> every pool entry rejected; reason blames the model pool)
body:
## Environment
- Hermes Agent v0.21.3 (2026.9.14, upstream `14efb460`), Windows 11
- hermes-jev 0.19.0
- Hermes provider declared as `custom` with `base_url: https://api.venice.ai/api/v1` (Venice behind Hermes' generic custom-provider config)
- Decision model reached via Venice: `jev doctor` reports `key.provider: venice`, `jev.reachable: true`
- `jev/state.json`: `routing: "on"`; `jev/routing.json`: all three tiers configured, `jev doctor` clean (`price_order: ok`, no dead specialty cells)

## Symptom
With routing on and pools configured, **every turn declines to route**, and the logged reason points at the model pools:

```json
{"kind":"route","mode":"on","from":"custom:deepseek-v4-1-flash","routed":false,
 "model":"custom:deepseek-v4-1-flash","tier":null,"specialty":null,
 "reason":"no simple model fits this turn","policy":"route-2"}
```

`"no simple model fits this turn"` sent me to re-check prices and pools, which were fine. The pools were never consulted.

## Root cause
`__init__.py:174` derives the provider from Hermes' name via the alias map:

```python
catalog_provider = catalog.HERMES_ALIASES.get(provider, provider)
```

Hermes passes `provider="custom"`, and `HERMES_ALIASES` (`jevkit/catalog.py:21`) has no entry for it, so `only_provider="custom"` is threaded into `route.decide()`. `_usable()` (`route.py:120-130`) requires `ref.split(":", 1)[0] == only_provider`, and every pool entry is `venice:...`. Nothing is selectable, so the router keeps the current model.

## Minimal repro (no gateway needed)
```python
from jevkit import route, catalog
catalog.HERMES_ALIASES.get("custom", "custom")          # -> 'custom'
route.decide("hello, what time is it", current="custom:deepseek-v4-1-flash",
             only_provider="custom", context_tokens=5000)
#    routed=False  reason='no simple model fits this turn'   <-- the log line
route.decide(..., only_provider="venice")   # routed=True  -> venice:mercury-2-5
route.decide(..., only_provider=None)       # routed=True  -> venice:mercury-2-5
```

## Impact
Total silent failure of routing on any install whose Hermes provider name is not a models.dev provider id. Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints are the common case: Venice behind `custom`, self-hosted vLLM/llama.cpp, gateways. Nothing warns; the only trace is a log reason that misdirects the reader to the model pools.

## Workaround
Add the mapping locally (`HERMES_ALIASES["custom"] = "venice"`). Verified working, but it is box-specific: a box with two `custom` providers would need resolution by model id rather than by provider name.

## Suggested fix
The provider filter exists so the router never swaps in a model the connected provider can't serve. When the catalog does not know the provider, filtering on it cannot achieve that goal, so the less-bad default is **no filter** (the pools are authored for the connected provider anyway) rather than no routing at all. Concretely, in `decide()`/`_pick()`:

- treat an `only_provider` that matches no catalog provider as `None`, and
- make the reason string distinguishable, e.g. `"no pool entry matches the connected provider (custom)"`, so this class of failure cannot be confused with a genuine model-fit miss.

Optionally allow the alias to be declared in `routing.json` (e.g. a `provider_aliases` key) so a custom endpoint can be mapped in config instead of by editing `catalog.py`.

title: pick-skill answers small talk with using-superpowers: remove meta-skills from the catalog and widen the local gate
body:
## Environment
Hermes Agent v0.21.3 (Windows 11), hermes-jev 0.19.0, 442 skills in the catalog (under the 960 cap).

## Symptom
On a labelled set of 17 turns - 12 with a known target skill, 5 that need none - both pure-chatter turns were answered with a skill, and the same one:

| turn | needs_skill | picked |
|---|---|---|
| `cool. next?` | 0.62 | `using-superpowers` |
| `hey how are you doing today` | 0.71 | `using-superpowers` |

No-skill accuracy was 3/5 (60%). This is the worst kind of false positive for `pick-skill`: `using-superpowers` is a meta-skill that tells the agent how to select and use skills, so it injects selector instructions into small talk where it looks harmless and is not.

Two separate causes:

1. **Meta-skills are in the catalog.** A skill whose job is to instruct the *selector* is not a procedure a turn can call for, but it is ranked like any other and can win.
2. **The local gate never sees these turns.** Only 1 of the 5 no-skill turns was answered locally for free ("thanks, that worked"). `cool. next?` is a pure continuation, but the question-mark test rejects it first - by design, since that test exists to keep real questions like "all working?" alive. `hey how are you doing today` fails the acknowledgement walk on "how", "doing" and "today".

## Suggested fix (implemented locally, measured)
**1. Remove meta-skills from the catalog** at the top of `pick()`, before the `MAX_SKILLS` slice so they do not consume batch slots either:

```python
META_SKILLS = frozenset((
    "using-superpowers", "skill-creator", "writing-skills", "writing-great-skills",
    "external-skill-analysis", "skill-factory", "skillclaw", "jev-skill-select",
))
# in pick(), first line: skills = [s for s in skills if s["name"] not in META_SKILLS]
```

**2. Two narrow additions to the local gate.**

- A continuation list checked *before* the question-mark test, matching only turns made entirely of those words: `next`, `and next`, `cool next`, `ok next`, `next one`, `go next`, `whats next`. Safety property kept: `next, fix the config` is still asked, as are `do it`, `go on to the next file` and `all working?`.
- Social openers added to `_ACK_PHRASES`: `how are you`, `how are you doing`, `how are you today`, `how are you doing today`, `hows it going`, `how is it going`, `how are things`, `hows things`, `good morning`, `good night`, `nice work`, `well done`.

One implementation note for anyone reusing this: the longest-phrase bound is derived with `_ACK_PHRASES | _CONTINUATION_PHRASES` (a union - `+` raises `TypeError` on frozensets).

## Measured after the guards (same 17-turn set)

- **turns needing no skill answered correctly: 3/5 -> 5/5**
- **meta-skill picks: 2 -> 0**
- **turns answered locally for free: 1/5 -> 3/5** ("cool. next?" and the greeting now cost 0 ms)
- the two that still reach Jev are deliberately kept: "what time is it" (a real question, nothing close so it ends after one request) and "ok do it" (a bare instruction)
- accuracy on the 12 target turns: unchanged

## Two documentation gaps found while measuring

1. **An empty `skills` list with `needs_skill` above the threshold is a normal reply, not a failure.** `ok do it` returned `status: ok`, `needs_skill: 0.55` and no skills - the second round trip read the finalists and rejected all of them. The reply table documents empty lists only for the trivial, nothing-close and fail-open cases, so this shape reads like a bug when it is stage 2 working.
2. **The "~1.1 s per turn" figure is provider-dependent.** Measured on this box: mean 4.3 s / median 5.2 s over 29 picks earlier in the day, then mean 1.1 s / median 1.2 s over 17 picks later the same day, with no change to the request path. Worth marking as an estimate rather than a property.

Happy to send this as a PR with the patch if useful. Local patch: `0002-jev-skillpick-guards.patch`.

title: hermes-jev plugin.yaml is missing `jev_search` and `provides_middleware`, so `hermes plugins validate` fails
body:
hermes-jev plugin.yaml is missing `jev_search` and `provides_middleware`, so `hermes plugins validate` fails



`hermes plugins validate` on the installed `hermes-jev` plugin fails on two
declaration checks, even though the plugin works correctly:

```
✓ loadable — entry: __init__.py
✓ python dependencies — none declared
✓ capability probe — register() ran in isolation
✗ declared tools — undeclared tools registered (not in provides_tools): jev_search
✓ declared hooks — matches registrations
✗ declared middleware — undeclared middleware registered (not in provides_middleware): llm_request
✓ built-in tool collisions — no collisions
```


`__init__.py` defines six tools in `_TOOLS` and registers all of them in
`register()`:

```
_TOOLS: jev_memory_filter, jev_search, jev_compact_select,
        jev_supervise, jev_escalate, jev_choose_action   (jev_search at line 364)
```

but `plugin.yaml` lists only five under `provides_tools` — `jev_search` is
absent.

`register()` also calls:

```python
ctx.register_hook("pre_llm_call", _on_pre_llm_call)          # line 479
ctx.register_hook("transform_llm_output", _on_transform_output)  # line 480
ctx.register_middleware("llm_request", _on_llm_request)      # line 481
```

`provides_hooks` declares both hooks, but `plugin.yaml` has no
`provides_middleware` key at all.


The runtime is unaffected — the plugin loads and behaves correctly. The cost
is on the validation/admission path: the catalog CI gate
(`hermes plugins validate`) cannot pass, so anyone packaging, mirroring or
vendoring this plugin hits a red gate for a packaging omission rather than a
real defect. It also hides the actual state of the plugin: a reader of
`plugin.yaml` cannot tell that `llm_request` middleware is installed, which is
the most invasive seam the plugin uses.


In `hermes/plugin/hermes-jev/plugin.yaml`:

```diff
 provides_tools:
   - jev_supervise
   - jev_escalate
   - jev_memory_filter
+  - jev_search
   - jev_compact_select
   - jev_choose_action
 provides_hooks:
   - pre_llm_call
   - transform_llm_output
+provides_middleware:
+  - llm_request
```

With that change, validation reports 12/13 passing, with the only remaining
failure being the security-scan item described below.


After the manifest fix, the only failing check is:

```
✗ security scan — dangerous: disregard_rules (rerank.py:405), dump_all_env
  (rerank.py:76), sudo_usage (rerank.py:68), sudo_usage (rerank.py:75),
  system_passwd_access (rerank.py:70)
```

All five point into `jevkit/rerank.py`, which is the prompt-injection
*screener* — the flagged strings are regex alternation members used to
**detect** attacks, not commands that execute. No `subprocess`/`eval` path
acts on matched text, and the only outbound hosts in the plugin are
`api.typesafe.ai`, `models.dev`, `openrouter.ai` and `github.com`.

The reason the guard does not recognise these as inert appears to be that
`is_regex_alternation_token` (in `tools/plugin_guard_context.py`) only treats a
token as inert when *every* occurrence on the line sits inside a literal and
reads as an alternation member. A short alternation passes:

```python
is_regex_alternation_token(finding, r'    r"foo|sudo|bar"')          # True
```

while the real, longer line fails because it stacks several risky tokens in one
regex (`\bbase64\b` next to `/etc/passwd`):

```python
is_regex_alternation_token(finding, r'    r"|\|\s*(?:sudo\s+)?(?:ba|z|da)?sh\b|\brm\s+-[a-z]*r[a-z]*f|\bbase64\b|/dev/tcp/|\bnc\s+-"')  # False
```

Raised only so a maintainer can confirm the intent; there is no inline
suppression mechanism (`noqa`/pragma) in the guard, so this is not something a
plugin author can resolve locally.


- Hermes Agent v0.21.4 (2026.9.21), install method: git
- hermes-jev 0.19.0 (plugin.yaml `manifest_version: 2`)
- Repo commit: e797a04
- Plugin scanner: plugin-guard-v8
- Linux, Python 3.12

title: Add OpenCode Zen as a Jev provider
body:
## What

TypeSafe is not accepting new signups, so a machine that has never held a Jev key cannot get one from them. OpenCode Zen serves the same Jev model on a free tier at the same kind of path (`/zen/v1/systemone`) with the same request body and the same `{"answers": {...}}` reply, so reaching it needs a provider entry, an endpoint, a model id and a transport — no new question, and no change to how a reply is validated.

Rebased onto today's `main`, so the provider list integrates with Venice (which landed while this was open): `PROVIDERS` becomes `("typesafe", "openrouter", "venice", "zen")`. Zen is appended *last* for the same reason Venice was — an install already resolving through any existing provider keeps doing exactly that when a Zen key appears; the existing Venice test is extended to pin the whole order (a machine holding Venice and Zen keys still resolves through Venice).

## Changes

First commit — the provider:

- `jevkit/keystore.py`: `PROVIDERS` gains `"zen"` (`OPENCODE_ZEN_API_KEY`, secret-store service `Hermes OpenCode Zen API`, its own `credentials-zen` file beside the TypeSafe one, like the other non-TypeSafe providers). New `JEV_PROVIDER` override: honoured only when it names a provider this machine can actually resolve a key for, so an unset, unknown or keyless value leaves the TypeSafe-first order exactly as it was.
- `jevkit/client.py`: `ZEN_ENDPOINT`, `ZEN_MODEL = "jev-1.13-free"`, `_zen_transport` (the TypeSafe request with none of OpenRouter's extra headers), and one lookup each for the per-provider model id and transport instead of the if/elif chain. The lookups resolve the module's names at call time — a table bound at import would freeze the transport functions and quietly defeat any caller or test that patches `client._openrouter_transport`, which is how the endpoint tests keep a request off the real network. The `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` endpoint path is untouched. Reply validation untouched.
- `jevkit/key_setup.py` and the `setup-key` help text: `jev setup-key --provider zen` knows what a Zen key is called and where it comes from, instead of saying "TypeSafe".
- `skills/jev-setup/SKILL.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`: how a person gets a Zen key, and how to pick the provider when more than one key is present.
- `tests/test_jevkit.py`: `ZenProviderTests` (4 tests) pins the model id, the URL, the absence of OpenRouter headers, the override beating a key for the default-preferred provider, that an unknown or keyless override does not move the order, and that each provider posts to its own URL and no other.

Second commit — the suite stops reading the developer's shell:

- A `JEV_PROVIDER` (or a provider key) exported in the developer's shell changes what `client.ask` does with no `provider=` argument: a different model id goes on the wire and a different transport is used. Two tests read that ambient state (the CLI/ask tests reached `_zen_transport` through a patched `_http_transport` that takes three arguments; the mailbox size test recomputed the model id from the environment), so the run was green on one shell and red on another with the same code — the failure mode CI cannot see.
- `tests/test_jevkit.py` now clears and restores `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` / `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` / `VENICE_API_KEY` / `OPENCODE_ZEN_API_KEY` / `TYPESAFE_MODEL` / `JEV_PROVIDER` for its own run, which is what its own comment already claimed. `tests/test_mailbox.py` reads the request-size gap off the request that was actually sent instead of recomputing it from the environment's model id.

No change to what any existing provider sends, to privacy filtering, to the fail-open paths, or to the reply validator. The README's "what leaves your machine" section is unchanged (a Zen install talks to `opencode.ai` instead of `api.typesafe.ai` — same body, fewer headers).

## How it was verified

Measured against OpenCode Zen, 2026-09-25:

- `GET /zen/v1/models` → 200, and `jev-1.13-free` is in the catalog (36 models, along with `jev-1.13`), so auth and the model id are real.
- The decision endpoint returned `429 FreeUsageLimitError` throughout that day (free-tier quota already spent, `retry-after` ≈ 8.6 h), which `_http_transport` maps to `JevError("rate_limited")` before the body reaches the validator. So the provider's success body has not yet been seen end-to-end against the live endpoint — stated plainly rather than implied. What was exercised instead: the full client path for provider `zen` (path, `"model": "jev-1.13-free"`, `Bearer`, no `X-Title`/`HTTP-Referer`, validated `answers`) against a local loopback server, and the real 429 coming back as `rate_limited`.

Suite (offline, stdlib only):

- `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` → **986 tests, OK** in all four shells tried: a TypeSafe key, a Zen key with `JEV_PROVIDER=zen`, a Venice key, and no provider key at all — on Python 3.13 and on Python 3.9. (Current `main` is 982 with the same result; this branch adds the 4 Zen tests.)
- `python3 -m unittest discover -s router-dashboard/tests` → 71 tests, OK (PyYAML installed).
- `python3 scripts/check_release.py` → `clean: 130 text files` (the same one binary PNG asks for an eyeball as on `main`).

title: Fix installer indentation when appending to plugins.enabled
body:
## The bug

`enable_plugins` recognised an `enabled:` key only at exactly two spaces, and it wrote the new plugin names at `  - ` whatever the file used. A hand-written `config.yaml` nests the list one level below the key:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
    - image_gen/openai-codex
    - orca-status
```

After an install, the file held:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
  - hermes-handoff
  - hermes-jev
    - image_gen/openai-codex
    - orca-status
```

which is not a list of four items. PyYAML reads it as **two** entries, the second one a folded string:

```python
>>> yaml.safe_load(open("config.yaml"))["plugins"]["enabled"]
['hermes-handoff', 'hermes-jev - image_gen/openai-codex - orca-status']
```

So `image_gen/openai-codex` and `orca-status` silently stopped being enabled, with no error anywhere — the file still looks like a list, and the installer reports success. Found on a real install (2026-09-25) of a config that had been written by hand. The block was repaired by hand on the spot; this PR is the fix the installer itself needed.

## The fix

- The `enabled:` key is found at any indentation (it was `^  enabled:`), so a block written deeper than two spaces is recognised instead of shadowed by a freshly inserted key.
- New names are written at the indentation the list itself already uses: the indentation of its existing items, or the key's own when the list is empty — the shape Hermes writes, and what the installer already produced for the two-space case.
- A `plugins:` block with no `enabled:` key gets the key at the block's own depth instead of always two spaces.
- Still a text edit of that one list: comments, ordering and every other setting survive, and nothing else in the file moves. The `enabled: []` → block-list conversion and the "already enabled" detection are unchanged; disabling still removes names at whatever indentation they sit.

Nothing else changes: the same backups are written, the same statuses reported, and no new file is read or written. Files already folded by the old installer are not rewritten automatically — the installer edits text and does not reparse YAML, so such a config still needs its indentation restored by hand; what changes is that it can no longer happen.

## The test

`tests/test_install.py`, new `IndentedBlockTests`:

- `test_a_nested_block_keeps_its_own_indentation` — the shape from the live install, asserted as text, plus an enable/disable round trip back to the original file byte for byte. Runs with or without PyYAML.
- `test_a_four_space_file_is_written_in_four_spaces` — a whole file indented at four spaces.
- `test_a_deeper_plugins_block_gets_its_enabled_key_at_its_own_depth` — `plugins:` at four spaces with no `enabled:` key.
- `test_the_fold_the_old_writing_caused_cannot_come_back` — with PyYAML: parses the exact text the previous installer produced (four plugins in, two entries out, one folded string) and then the fixed output (all four names). Skips cleanly where PyYAML is absent.

Verified that the tests catch the bug: with `install.py` at `main`, all four fail; with the fix, all four pass.

## How it was verified

- `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` → 944 tests, OK, on Python 3.9 and 3.13 (current `main` is 940 plus these four).
- The fold and the fixed result were reproduced with PyYAML against the real `enable_plugins` before and after the change, not against a hand-built string; the hand-built string in the test is the exact old output, pinned so it cannot come back.
- `python3 -m unittest discover -s router-dashboard/tests` → 71 tests, OK; `python3 scripts/check_release.py` → `clean: 126 text files` (the same one binary PNG as on `main`).

## One deliberate extra

`.github/workflows/test.yml`: `pip install pyyaml` moves above the suite so the fold check runs in CI instead of skipping (the job already installed PyYAML one step later for the dashboard tests). If you would rather keep the first step stdlib-only, drop that hunk: the three text tests still fail on the old behaviour without a parser, and the PyYAML one skips.

title: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL: an authenticated HTTPS gateway under a path prefix is unusable (path refused, no credential sent)
body:
## What I hit

A self-hosted gateway that fronts Jev (`https://gw.example/jev`, mandatory `Authorization`
bearer) cannot be used with `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` today, in two independent ways: a base URL that
carries a path is refused before any request goes out, and an override host never receives the
credential the gateway requires. Every call fails, and every caller fails open silently — it
reads as "Jev had no opinion", not as a configuration error.

## Verified at

- Upstream `origin/main` = `085e5c652bf4f1c65e8b064c84515a519c8df6a4` (2026-09-25 13:10:32 -0500)
- The same behaviour observed locally on `5b4dd7b`, based on that commit

## Reproduction (offline, at the verified SHA)

```
$ python3 -c "
from jevkit import client
try:
    print('accepted ->', client._custom_typesafe_endpoint('https://gw.example/jev'))
except Exception as e:
    print('rejected:', type(e).__name__, e)
"
rejected: JevError invalid_endpoint
```

`jevkit/client.py:300` rejects any `parsed.path` other than `/`, so a gateway's mandatory
prefix cannot be named at all. Drop the prefix and the request does go out — carrying nothing:

```
$ # real local recording server, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=<its url>, TYPESAFE_API_KEY set in the env
path the client requested: /v1/systemone
Authorization header the proxy received: None
```

That is `jevkit/client.py:499` (`key = None if endpoint else api_key or keystore.resolve(via)`),
and `tests/test_custom_endpoint.py:14` and `:60` pin it deliberately. Against a gateway that
requires a bearer the answer is HTTP 401, which `ask()` returns as no information: the
documented fail-open path, reached for a reason the operator cannot see from the outside.

## Expected

The official TypeSafe SDKs read `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and pair it with `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the
same environment. For an *explicit* `https://` override I would expect:

- a path prefix to be part of the endpoint (`https://gw.example/jev/v1/systemone`), not a
  validation error;
- the bearer to be `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the process environment — the same value the SDK
  would send, and nothing else: never a keychain entry, never a credentials file.

Loopback `http://` mocks keep receiving no credential at all, and non-loopback `http` stays
refused. Those parts of #15 are right and this report does not ask for them to change.

## Relation to existing work

- #15 asked for `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and was closed as addressed at
  `8691252b6a141413347973c18f93e67ffeefde19` with the explicit guarantee of "no provider-key
  forwarding". This is **not** a claim that the guard was overlooked: it is deliberate, it is
  documented in `skills/jev-setup/SKILL.md`, and this report is a request to revisit one
  consequence of it — an authenticated compatible endpoint, which is an endpoint the SDK
  convention supports, has no supported configuration at all.
- Searches run over issues and PRs for `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, `proxy`, `bearer`, `base url`:
  only #15 matches, and its own body scopes it to a keyless local server ("a local server
  ignores the bearer token").
- Discriminator: #15 covers a keyless mock; this covers an endpoint that requires exactly the
  key the SDK would send, over `https`, with a path prefix.

## Scope of the credential question

Nothing is read from disk by the proposed change: the bearer would come from `os.environ` only.
An operator who sets `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` has already put that key into
that process's environment — that is how the SDK is configured — so the change does not widen
where a *stored* key can reach, it makes the documented SDK pairing work. If the no-forwarding
guarantee is nonetheless meant to cover authenticated proxies too, saying so in `SKILL.md`
("a proxy that requires a credential is not supported") would save the next operator the 401;
I would rather have the decision stated than the gap.

## Suggested fix location

`jevkit/client.py:_custom_typesafe_endpoint` for the path rule, and the key choice in `ask()` —
one small helper, no new machinery, no new configuration key. A branch with the change and a
test is ready; I will open it as a draft PR so the design question can be settled before review.

Redaction: the gateway is `https://gw.example/jev`, the key synthetic, the hostname generic;
nothing from a real machine is in this report.

I read `SECURITY.md` before filing: this is not a disclosure — nothing leaves the machine today,
and the request is to send a value the operator has already put into that process's environment.
If you would rather settle the credential boundary privately, close this and say so and I will
take it there.

title: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL: allow an https path prefix and send the env TYPESAFE_API_KEY as its bearer
body:
<!-- Thank you. A short PR with a test beats a long one without. -->

Refs #23 — deliberately not `Fixes`, for the reason in "The open question": this narrows a
guarantee stated in #15's close comment, so the decision matters more than the diff.

## What this changes

`TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` can now name an authenticated HTTPS gateway under a path prefix. What went
wrong: a gateway that both mounts the API under a prefix and requires a bearer had no workable
configuration — the path was refused as `invalid_endpoint` before any request went out, and an
override host was sent no credential at all, so such a gateway answered 401 to every call and
every caller failed open silently.

**`5b4dd7b` — `jevkit/client.py`, `tests/test_custom_endpoint.py`**

- `_custom_typesafe_endpoint`: an `https` base URL may carry a path prefix. `http` may not;
  non-loopback cleartext, userinfo, query, fragment and port 0 stay refused.
- new `_proxy_env_key(endpoint)`: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from `os.environ` when the override is
  `https://`, `None` otherwise.
- `ask()`: for a custom endpoint the key is `_proxy_env_key(...)` where it used to be a hard
  `None`. `api_key` and `keystore.resolve` are still never consulted when an override is in use.
- one new test, `test_https_proxy_gets_env_key_only_never_a_stored_credential`.

**`044e8ec` — CONTRIBUTING's sync rule for a change to what is sent to Jev**

- the `## Unreleased` CHANGELOG entry, and the one sentence in `skills/jev-setup/SKILL.md` that
  would otherwise still say no credential is ever forwarded to an override endpoint. The fix
  commit is untouched.

## Why

A self-hosted LiteLLM pass-through in front of Jev is the case: `https://<gateway>/jev`, bearer
required. With `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` set, the client either refused the URL outright or sent no
`Authorization` header — and a 401 from the gateway reaches the caller as "no information", which
is fail-open working as designed while hiding the reason completely. Both halves, reproduced
offline at `085e5c6`:

```
$ python3 -c "from jevkit import client; client._custom_typesafe_endpoint('https://gw.example/jev')"
JevError: invalid_endpoint

$ # local recording server; TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=<its url>, TYPESAFE_API_KEY set in the environment
path the client requested: /v1/systemone
Authorization header the proxy received: None
```

## How it was checked

- [ ] `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` passes — **not on this machine, and not because of
      this change.** 1021 tests, `FAILED (failures=3, errors=1)`. The identical four fail at the
      base commit `085e5c6` under the same command
      (`test_route_health.SkillHookRootTests` ×3 and
      `test_gui_agent.CredentialIsolationTests.test_selected_transport_and_authorization_follow_key_provenance`),
      so it is left unticked rather than claimed green. Both runs had
      `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`/`TYPESAFE_API_KEY` unset in the shell.
- [x] `python3 scripts/check_release.py` is clean — `clean: 135 text files`, with the usual
      `NOT SCANNED (1 binary): docs/images/model-routing-dashboard.png`.
- [x] A test that fails before this change and passes after —
      `test_https_proxy_gets_env_key_only_never_a_stored_credential`. Against `085e5c6` with only
      the new test file in place: `FAILED (errors=1)`, `KeyError: 'Authorization'`. On this head:
      ```
      $ python3 -m unittest -q tests.test_custom_endpoint
      Ran 7 tests in 0.040s
      OK
      $ python3 -m unittest discover -s router-dashboard/tests
      Ran 71 tests in 2.200s
      OK
      ```
- [ ] Ran it against real Jev — **no.** What I ran is the offline pair above. The gateway that
      motivated this needs the operator's key in the environment to answer, and I am not going to
      spend someone else's key on a PR. The header the client builds for an `https` override is
      pinned by the new test instead.

## The two things reviewers will look at first

- [x] **Nothing new leaves the machine, with one thing named exactly.** On an explicit `https://`
      override with a path, the request now carries
      `Authorization: Bearer <TYPESAFE_API_KEY from that same process environment>`. Nothing else
      moves: no content field changes, no destination becomes reachable that the operator did not
      name, and no credential is read from a keychain, `~/.config/jev/credentials` or any file. The
      value configured for the official SDK is the value sent — that is the whole change. The
      README's "What leaves your machine" section is about prompt content and is not extended by
      this. A loopback `http://` override still receives no `Authorization` header at all and
      non-loopback cleartext is still refused, so a slip in the variable cannot turn into a key
      over plaintext.
- [x] **It fails open.** No new raise path: an override endpoint with the variable unset yields no
      header, exactly as before, and a key is still only required when there is no override at all.
      The endpoint validator accepts strictly more inputs than before. Nothing here raises into a
      caller that did not raise before.

## The open question

#15's close comment states the guarantee as "no provider-key forwarding". This PR narrows that
guarantee deliberately rather than repairing an oversight. If it is meant to hold for
authenticated proxies too, close this and I will not argue the change — in that case the only ask
is a line in `SKILL.md` saying a credential-requiring proxy is not supported, so the next operator
does not spend an afternoon on a 401.

CI: no run observed for this head, and nothing claimed about it. If the four failures above are
this machine's, CI should be green; if they are not, that is a fact about `main` rather than about
this branch.

Found while wiring a self-hosted LiteLLM/Jev pass-through. Every host in this text is a
placeholder and the key in it is synthetic.

title: web-screen catch does not transfer across public attack sets
body:
Target: `kerpopule/hermes-jev-skills`
Pinned source: `cf9e84cb363c4a6257adea9d1ddf2a7420bcc434`

## Dedupe

We searched the repository's open and closed issues for `webscreen`, `prompt injection`, and `jev`.
No existing issue describes cross-corpus web-screen catch-rate transfer. Related closed issues
#3 (routing cache/compaction bytes), #4 (plugin routing hook), #8 (plugin installation), #18,
and #20 (plugin metadata) are distinct. This draft is one defect: generalization of the
web-screen catch rate, not plugin loading, routing cache, or threshold tuning.

## Observation

The published scorecard's own planted attacks are not a transferable estimate of web-screen recall.
On the exact same model/question family and fresh public inputs:

| Attack set | Caught | Wilson 95% interval | Receipt |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Hermes own attacks | 68/78 = 87.2% | 77.98–92.88% | `work/hermes-webscreen-repro/RECEIPT.md` / `5c17a18c` |
| `deepset/prompt-injections` descriptive set | 135/256 = 52.7% | 46.62–58.76% | `work/hermes-webscreen-repro/RECEIPT.md` / `5c17a18c` |
| Fresh S-Labs test split | 15/40 = 37.5% | 24.22–52.97% | `work/omp-hermes-screen/hermes-own-live-receipt-20260926.json` / `1b3b0a9b` |

The fresh S-Labs arm is especially important because Hermes's own `jevkit.webscreen.screen()`
implementation and the frozen TypeScript port both caught **15/40**, with paired McNemar
`b=1`, `c=1`, exact two-sided `p=1.0`. The clean side was zero false positives in both arms.
That parity means the lower fresh-set result is not evidence that our port alone is weak.

The Hermes own arm used 81 pinned `jev-1.13.0` calls and 122,011 input tokens in the first
attempt; the corrected exact-clean rerun used 81 calls, 118,794 input tokens, and **$0.004989348**.
Total parity investigation spend, including the discarded clean-wrapper attempt, was
**$0.010113810**. No paid comparator ran.

## Why this is actionable

The scorecard's 87.5–89.7% number is valid for its own planted attack family, but a user deploying
this as a web-result screen needs a public, held-out attack distribution. The fresh public result
has a wide interval and is not a definitive ranking claim, but the point estimate and interval are
far below the published own-attack result. A fixed threshold and local screen cannot be described as
having portable recall from the own-attack score alone.

Suggested upstream actions:

1. Keep the own-attack scorecard, but label it **in-distribution planted recall**.
2. Add a permanently versioned public held-out attack set and report its prevalence and Wilson
   interval separately.
3. Report clean false positives and fail-open rows for every attack set.
4. Do not tune the threshold on the public set; preregister a second held-out set for threshold
   changes.
5. Preserve the exact question/model/provider and report the model-returned id, not only the sent id.

## Reproduction references

The lane preregistration and frozen input hashes are in:

- `work/hermes-webscreen-repro/PREREG.md` amendment `jev-qe5h`;
- `var/agent-tmp/jev-vrbl-fresh-20260926/meta.json` (attack and clean SHA-256s);
- `work/omp-hermes-screen/FRESH-PREREG-20260926.md` / `8450b8d2`;
- `work/omp-hermes-screen/fresh-live-receipt-20260926.json` / `98169a1e`;
- `work/hermes-webscreen-repro/hermes-own-live-receipt-20260926.json` / `1b3b0a9b`.

Raw attack/page text remains local and is not part of this draft.

## Boundary

This draft is not filed. It is not a claim that Hermes is unusable, not a model-quality ruling,
and not evidence that the fresh S-Labs set is representative of all web attacks. It identifies a
measurement/reporting gap: a favorable in-distribution score cannot stand alone for deployment
recall.

title: catalog: add Nous Portal from its own /models
body:
## Summary
- models.dev has no Nous entry, so models served through Nous Portal never showed up in `jev models list` / pool suggestions.
- `jevkit/catalog.py` adds a `nous` provider from the Nous inference API's OpenRouter-shaped `/models`. It is fetched only on `refresh` — routing reads the catalog every turn and must not hit the network — and saved to the cache dir. Without a saved copy it falls back to Hermes's `provider_models_cache.json` Nous list priced from models.dev's OpenRouter entry; with neither, no Nous provider is added. `:batch` ids and variable-priced (-1) routers are dropped. If models.dev ever lists Nous itself, that entry wins.
- The `models suggest --provider` fix is now its own PR, per review.

## What leaves the machine (for owner review)
- Only on `refresh`: the Hermes Nous login from `auth.json` (`agent_key`, then `access_token`) as `Authorization: Bearer …` to `inference_base_url + "/models"`.

title: skillpick.discover() skips skills in symlinked folders (Path.rglob does not follow symlinks)
body:
### What happened, and what you expected instead

`skillpick.discover()` walks each root with `root.rglob("SKILL.md")` (`jevkit/skillpick.py:116`). `Path.rglob` does not descend into symlinked directories, so any skill that is linked into a skills root instead of copied there is silently left out of the catalog. `pick` can then never suggest it, and nothing reports the loss.

This is a common layout. On my machine, `~/.claude/skills` has 37 skills that are symlinks into a folder shared by Claude Code, Codex and Hermes. None of the 37 were discovered. I found it while replaying past turns through `pick` in shadow mode, when two skills that were clearly the right answer were missing from the catalog.

I expected skills behind a symlinked folder to be discovered like any other skill.

### The smallest way to see it again

```bash
D=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$D/shared/watch" "$D/root/local"
printf -- '---\nname: watch\ndescription: x\n---\n' > "$D/shared/watch/SKILL.md"
printf -- '---\nname: local\ndescription: y\n---\n' > "$D/root/local/SKILL.md"
ln -s "$D/shared/watch" "$D/root/watch"
python3 -c "
import sys; from pathlib import Path; sys.path.insert(0, '.')
from jevkit import skillpick
print(sorted(s['name'] for s in skillpick.discover([Path('$D/root')])))"
```

Run from the repo root. It prints `['local']`; expected `['local', 'watch']`.

### A possible fix

`rglob(..., recurse_symlinks=True)` exists only on Python 3.13+, and the repo supports 3.9. `os.walk(root, followlinks=True)` works on 3.9. It needs a guard against symlink cycles (a link pointing back at an ancestor), for example by skipping any directory whose `os.path.realpath` has already been visited. The existing dot-folder, `quarantine` and `node_modules` filters can be applied to `dirnames` in place, which also stops the walk from entering them.

A test could build the tree above in a temp dir and assert that `watch` is found, plus a second case with a link back to the root to show the walk terminates.

### Output of `jev doctor`

Not installed on this machine. I imported `jevkit` from a clone and called `discover()` directly.

### Version

Commit `cf9e84c` (latest `main` as of 2026-09-27). The line is unchanged since `8691252`.

### Where it runs

Claude Code (also affects Codex and Hermes whenever a skills root contains symlinked skill folders)

### OS and Python version

macOS, Python 3.14.7

title: Windows without Developer Mode: `install.py` creates no `jev` lane (symlink-only, no fallback)
body:
### What happens

On Windows without Developer Mode or admin rights, `install.py` cannot install the
`jev` CLI at all. Symlink creation is denied and there is no fallback:

```
could not be linked: A required privilege is not held by the client
```

`os.symlink` raises:

```
OSError [WinError 1314] A required privilege is not held by the client
```

So `~/.local/bin/jev` (and any `--hermes-home` lane) is never created.

### Why

`install.py` links lanes with `link.symlink_to(target)` (see `_link_command`,
`install.py:67` and `install.py:122`), and `os.link(` appears in **no** revision of
`install.py` — `git log -S'os.link(' -- install.py` is empty, and `symlink_to` has
been the only link mechanism since the very first commit `191a715` (0.1.0).
There is no copy/hardlink fallback, so a host that cannot make symlinks gets nothing.

Measured on the affected host (Windows 11 26200, git-bash/MSYS):

| Mechanism | Result |
|---|---|
| `os.symlink` / `mklink` | denied — WinError 1314 / "insufficient privilege" |
| `mklink /H` (hard link, files) | **works** (`nlink=2`) |
| `mklink /J` (junction, dirs) | **works** (reparse tag 2684354563) |
| git-bash `ln -s` | silently **copies** (not a link) |

Hardlinks and junctions need no elevation — either would let the installer work here.
This is the established fallback pattern elsewhere, not a novel ask:

- **uv** ships a `link-mode` setting that **defaults to hardlink on Windows** and
  explicitly discourages symlinks (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings).
- **pnpm** hit this identical failure and fixed it with a junction fallback:
  `os error 1314` → junctions (https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13694).
  Its `symlink-dir` package documents the rule verbatim: *"Uses 'junctions' on
  Windows if 'symbolic links' is disallowed. Even though support for 'symbolic
  links' was added in Vista+, users by default lack permission to create them."*
  (https://unpkg.com/symlink-dir@10.0.3/README.md)
- **CPython #104046** covers the sibling bug (`shutil.copytree` does not understand
  NTFS junctions), which is the same failure mode as this repo's `_copytree` →
  `shutil.rmtree(dst)` refusing a link
  (https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/104046).
- Microsoft documents both the privilege and its Developer Mode unlock:
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/hard-links-and-junctions

### Compounding detail

`_link_command` deliberately refuses to replace a `jev` it did not create
(`is a file this installer did not put there`), which is the right call. But combined
with the above it means a lane that already exists as a plain copy is **never**
repaired by the installer, and the copied lane's `readlink -f "$0"` has no symlink
target to follow, so `$here` resolves to the lane's own directory and the CLI dies
with `No module named jevkit`.

### Suggested fix (small)

After `link.symlink_to(target)` raises `OSError`, fall back in order:

1. `shutil.copy2(JEV, link)` — a real copy always works, and the guard already keeps
   the installer from overwriting anything it did not make;
2. optionally try `os.link(JEV, link)` first where it is cheap, but note the shim must
   then not depend on `readlink -f` to locate `jevkit` (in `bin/jev`, follow `$0` only
   when `-L` says it is a real symlink, then search the known install locations).

Reporting the failure as a warning rather than `could not be linked` alone would also
make the Windows case diagnosable.

### Environment- Windows 11 build 26200, git-bash (MSYS), Python 3.10, **no Developer Mode, no admin**
- repo at `c528375` (v0.22.0)
- `os.symlink` probe: `python -c "import os,tempfile; os.symlink(tempfile.mkdtemp()+'/t', tempfile.mkdtemp()+'/l')"`

title: fix: floor the effort pick by tier and guard catalog-unknown refs at large context
body:
Three failures measured on a live Hermes fleet, one fix each. All three are fail-open-safe and ship behind the existing `effort`/`tiers` config, so nothing changes for a setup that has not opted in.

**1. The effort pick could undercut the routing tier.**

Routing decides the tier from probability *mass*; `effort.pick` reads the single largest *bucket*. The two can disagree — a turn routing called `medium` can still have `trivial` as its argmax. Observed live: a tool-needing turn got the cheapest thinking budget and answered in one line with **zero tool calls**. `tier_floor` / `min_bucket_for` now floor the pick by the tier, and a low-confidence *kept* decision floors too ("unsure is not hard" cuts both ways). A confident trivial turn is unchanged, so the cheap tier stays cheap.

**2. The large-context guard never ran for catalog-unknown refs.**

`_pick` trusts a ref the models.dev catalog does not know (every local relay — `omniproxy:*` and friends). Those rows carry no `price`, so the `picked_price < current_price` comparison silently skipped and **every** large-context turn still switched models onto a cold cache — which measured *slower* on a per-request-billed relay where cost is identical either way. `_large_context_verdict` now fails safe and keeps the current model when either price is unknown; effort routing still applies, because `_keep` carries the answers out.

**3. The decision cache leaked across the guard.**

The cache key buckets context, and a bucket straddling `sticky_context_tokens` let a cached sub-guard SWITCH answer an over-guard turn (a session growing past the threshold kept switching). `_sticky_side` puts the guard's own boundary in the key, using the same **strict `>`** as `decide()` — a `>=` here reintroduces the leak at the boundary.

27 tests in `tests/test_effort_floor_and_sticky_guard.py` pin all three, including the boundary at the threshold, the priced-guard-still-runs-first path, and every fail-open branch. Full suite: `python -m unittest discover -s tests` → 1393 tests OK.

While writing them, one test caught a real bug in `min_bucket_for` itself: it called `.get("tier")` before the `isinstance(decision, Mapping)` check, so a non-mapping decision raised `AttributeError` instead of failing open. Fixed here.

title: plugin.yaml declares only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, but keystore.py resolves any of four provider keys
body:
## `requires_env` under-declares the key the plugin actually needs

`hermes/plugin/hermes-jev/plugin.yaml` declares:

```yaml
requires_env:
  - TYPESAFE_API_KEY
```

But `jevkit/keystore.py` supports **four** providers and resolves any of their keys:

```python
PROVIDERS = ("typesafe", "openrouter", "venice", "zen")
_ENV = {"typesafe": ENV_VAR, "openrouter": "OPENROUTER_API_KEY",
        "venice": "VENICE_API_KEY", "zen": "OPENCODE_ZEN_API_KEY"}
```

So an install running entirely on OpenRouter — which the module docstring at
`client.py:397` explicitly anticipates, and which the Venice/OpenCode-Zen support was
added for — satisfies the plugin's real requirement while the manifest claims a key
that is not present and not needed.

## Why this matters (it is not just cosmetic)

`requires_env` is what drives the install-time prompt
(`hermes_cli/plugin_packs.py:20`, `:389`). An OpenRouter user gets prompted for a
TypeSafe key they do not have and do not want. If they skip it, the manifest now
misrepresents the install's state to anything that reads it.

Concretely, this cost real time here: an audit reading `requires_env`, finding no
`TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the environment, and concluding Jev was dead. It was not —
`jev-serve` reported `state: ready`, `key_src: ~/.hermes/.env` (OpenRouter), and the
plugin was `enabled` and answering. The manifest was the only thing saying otherwise.

## Suggested fix

Declare the real requirement rather than one provider's spelling. Options, in the
order I would pick them:

1. **Declare all four** — accurate, and the installer prompt then reads as "any one of
   these":
   ```yaml
   requires_env:
     - TYPESAFE_API_KEY
     - OPENROUTER_API_KEY
     - VENICE_API_KEY
     - OPENCODE_ZEN_API_KEY
   ```
   Caveat: I do not know whether `requires_env` is "all of these" or "any of these" in
   the loader. If it is "all", this is wrong and option 2 is the one to take.

2. **Drop `requires_env` and document the provider choice in the description**, since
   resolution is genuinely a runtime concern handled by `keystore.py` (including the
   `JEV_PROVIDER` override). The plugin loads and works with no `requires_env` at all —
   verified here, where the declaration is unsatisfied and the plugin still loads.

3. **Add a `providers`-style field** if the manifest schema has room for an
   any-of/one-of secret requirement, and point `requires_env` at that.

I lean to (2) as the smallest correct change, but (1) is right if the loader supports
any-of semantics and the prompt UX is worth it.

## Environment where this was observed

- `hermes-jev` 0.22.0 installed; upstream `main` is 0.22.1 and has the same
  `requires_env` block, so this is not fixed by upgrading.
- Jev reached through OpenRouter: `~/.hermes/.env` carries `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`,
  `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` absent.
- `jev-serve` health: `{"state": "ready", "model": "typesafe/jev-1.13",
  "key_src": "~/.hermes/.env"}` — decisions working, skill routing verified end to end
  (it correctly ranked a 314-skill catalog and still returned *no skill* for small talk).
- Hermes Agent 0.21.5, WSL2.

Happy to open the PR for whichever option you prefer — say which and I will send it.

title: pinned is read from a spelling mismatch with model.default: routing no-ops on 72% of turns in one profile
body:
Measured on one Hermes machine (macOS, Hermes profile `default`, plugin `hermes-jev` 0.23.0, routing in `shadow`), over the 24 h to 2026-10-11 08:00:

- 592 decision rows, all from profile `default`.
- **428 of them (72 %) read `reason: "you pinned this model"`** — the person never ran `/model`.
- 54 more read `no medium model fits this turn` (the session's provider, `commandcode`, names no models.dev provider, so no pool entry passes `_usable`; a different, already-known class).
- 114 read `low confidence 0.2x`.

## What is happening

The profile's Hermes config resolves to

```yaml
model:
  provider: commandcode
  default: deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash
```

The same model is also reached through a second endpoint (a Hermes `custom` provider, `provider_aliases.custom = tokenharbor`), and on that path the hook receives the endpoint's own model id — `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, no vendor prefix. The two paths alternate, so the fnmatch-style comparison in `hermes/plugin/hermes-jev/__init__.py` (lines 455-469) sees:

```
bare         = "deepseek-v4.1-flash"          # from model=f"tokenharbor:deepseek-v4.1-flash"
default_bare = "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash" # str(model.default).split(":", 1)[-1]
pinned       = bool(default_bare) and bare != default_bare   # -> True
```

`split(":", 1)[-1]` normalises a `provider:model` default, but not a `vendor/model` default, and not a bare id against a `vendor/model` default. The same turn on the `commandcode` path arrives as `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` and compares equal, so *which* of the two endpoints serves the turn decides whether it looks pinned.

Evidence for the split, all inside one hour of the log (same profile, same visible model):

```
kind=route  from="tokenharbor:deepseek-v4.1-flash"        reason="you pinned this model"
kind=route  from="commandcode:deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash" reason="no medium model fits this turn"
```

## Why it matters

`pinned` is the user's explicit choice ("you ran `/model`: your choice wins"), and it is the one switch that must never be wrong in the *permissive* direction from a routing standpoint — every false positive silently removes a turn from routing. On this machine it removes three quarters of them, and the reason string in the log blames the person, so it reads as intended behaviour to anyone auditing decisions.

## Suggested direction

Compare like with like: normalise both sides before deciding (drop a leading `<provider>:`, and when both strings contain `/`, compare the vendor prefix and the tail separately rather than comparing one full string against the other's tail). A model id Hermes itself resolved for the profile would be even better than re-deriving the default from `config.yaml`.

title: jev spend --hermes-db reports "no usage": the messages table no longer has a model column (data is in session_model_usage)
body:
## Summary

`jev spend --hermes-db <state.db>` prints `no usage: pass --usage <export.json> and/or --hermes-db <state.db>` on this machine, i.e. the flag looks ignored. The cause is a Hermes schema change: the reader still expects a `model` column on the `messages` table, which this Hermes build no longer has. The data now lives in `session_model_usage`.

## Where it fails

`jevkit/spend.py`, `from_hermes_sessions()`:

```python
columns = {r[1] for r in conn.execute("pragma table_info(messages)")}
if not {"role", "timestamp"} <= columns:
    return []
model_col = "model" if "model" in columns else None
token_col = "token_count" if "token_count" in columns else None
if not (model_col and token_col):
    return []
```

`messages` still has `role`, `timestamp` and `token_count`, but **not** `model`, so `model_col` is `None` and the function returns `[]` for every profile. The CLI then reports "no usage" even though `--hermes-db` was passed.

## Measured here (2026-10-12)

```
$ sqlite3 "file:$HOME/.hermes/state.db?mode=ro" "pragma table_info(messages);"
id|session_id|role|content|tool_call_id|tool_calls|tool_name|timestamp|token_count|
finish_reason|reasoning|...            # no `model` column

$ jev spend --days 7 --hermes-db ~/.hermes/state.db
no usage: pass --usage <export.json> and/or --hermes-db <state.db>
```

The per-model data is in `session_model_usage` (13,363 rows here), one row per session × model × provider:

```
session_id, model, billing_provider, billing_base_url, billing_mode, task,
api_call_count, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens,
reasoning_tokens, estimated_cost_usd, actual_cost_usd, cost_status, cost_source,
first_seen, last_seen
```

Aggregating that table by hand for the last 7 days gives exactly what `spend` is supposed to print: 2,950 API calls, 13.2M input tokens, 1.83M output tokens, 154.7M cache-read tokens (92.1% cache hit), split by model and billing provider:

| model | billing_provider | calls | in | out | cache-read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| deepseek-v4.1-flash | custom | 1646 | 8,992,508 | 637,269 | 38,260,352 |
| deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash | commandcode | 1174 | 3,407,108 | 1,122,766 | 102,748,800 |
| gpt-6.1-sol | openai-codex | 95 | 688,752 | 55,059 | 9,907,456 |
| deepseek-flash | deepseek | 34 | 135,207 | 19,398 | 3,744,128 |

## Suggested fix

Prefer `session_model_usage` when the table exists (it carries the model, the billing provider and the cache split per session), and keep the `messages` path as the fallback for databases that predate it. `estimated_cost_usd` / `actual_cost_usd` are present but `0.0` with `cost_status = unknown` here, so the value of the rows is the token counts, not the dollars.

title: Add image support and a TypeSafe Jev vision shadow
body:
## What this changes

Adds support for TypeSafe's new images preview ("Dreamer-ready", docs.typesafe.ai/images) and puts it to use in one place, behind its own switch.

- **`jevkit/images.py`** reads a PNG or JPEG header and refuses, before anything is sent, every picture the API would refuse: wrong format, animated PNG, progressive or non-baseline JPEG, sides outside 256–1568 px, pixel count out of range, over 16 MiB, or a JPEG whose EXIF orientation rotates it (the API ignores EXIF, so the model would see it on its side). Standard library only, so it never resizes anything.
- **`client.ask(..., assets=...)`** sends images with the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true` header, to TypeSafe or an explicit `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` only. OpenRouter, Venice and Zen get `images_unsupported` without anything being sent. An image the request never refers to is refused locally instead of coming back as a 400. Requests over 32 MiB are refused too.
- **`client.box()`** adds the new Box question. The answer is checked: each edge between 0 and 1, `left < right`, `top < bottom`.
- **`jevkit/cloud_vision.py`** with `/jev vision_cloud shadow`: TypeSafe Jev answers the same pass/fail and yes/no `vision_analyze` questions the local Jev-Omni shadow answers. It logs to the same `logs/jev-vision.jsonl` with `model: typesafe-jev`, so the two can be compared.
- **`scripts/live_images_check.py`**: one live request about a drawn square with a known answer, asking a Noul, a Choice and a Box.
- **`scripts/vision_cloud_ab.py`**: accuracy, plus coverage and accuracy at each confidence cut-off, on hand-labelled checks. It's for setting `THRESHOLD`, which is borrowed from Jev-Omni's 0.6 for now.
- Docs in `docs/images.md`, an entry in the README's "What leaves your machine" section, and a CHANGELOG line. The version is not bumped (left for the release steward).

## Why

TypeSafe now accepts images. The vision shadow already collects exactly the decisions an image-capable Jev could take over: pass/fail and yes/no questions about a picture. This lets TypeSafe Jev be measured on them next to Jev-Omni and the helper model, without changing any result.

- [x] `python3 scripts/check_release.py` is clean
- [x] New tests in `tests/test_images_and_cloud_vision.py` (25):

  - **Client:** assets and header sent, text-only requests unchanged, unreferenced asset refused, non-TypeSafe providers refused, box validated.
  - **Real HTTP:** full requests over a socket to a local stand-in that enforces the documented rules, with a 1568×1500 image plus a Box question, and two images in one request.

title: fix: carry effort inside reasoning on the Codex Responses wire
body:
## What broke

With effort routing on, the `llm_request` middleware wrote a top-level `reasoning_effort` onto every routed turn. Chat-completions wires accept that field, but the Codex Responses wire carries effort inside `reasoning.effort`, and its preflight rejects a top-level `reasoning_effort` as a **non-retryable client error** — so every routed turn on that wire died after retries with `Codex Responses request has unsupported field(s): reasoning_effort`.

Observed live on a Hermes gateway: routed turns aborted mid-turn; the failure sat between the two preflight layers (middleware runs after the first preflight), so it only surfaced as a terminal ValueError.

## The fix

`_with_effort` now detects the Responses payload (`input` present, no `messages`) and merges the level into the `reasoning` object, preserving sibling keys (`summary`, caps, ...). When `reasoning` is absent on that wire — reasoning disabled — the request is left alone instead of re-enabling reasoning the caller had turned off. Chat wires keep the top-level field exactly as before.

## Tests

- Two middleware cases on the Responses wire: reasoning present (merged, siblings kept, no top-level field) and reasoning disabled (request untouched).
- Full suite green: 1512 passed, 1 skipped, 411 subtests.

title: Model routing can select a model with a different API protocol, causing ModelProtocolUnsupported
body:
### What happened, and what you expected instead

## Environment
* **hermes-jev:** `0.25.1`
* **Integration:** Hermes with OpenCode Go
* **Routing:** Jev model routing enabled (`/jev routing on`)
* **Model State:** Current model: `glm-5.3-flash`; routed candidate: `grok-4.7`

---

## Problem Summary
The Jev router can select a model served by the same provider but requiring a different API protocol. In this case, the plugin swapped `request.model` to `grok-4.7`, while the request still hit OpenCode Go's Chat Completions endpoint:

`/zen/go/v1/chat/completions`

The provider returned an HTTP 400 error:
`ModelProtocolUnsupported: Model does not support this protocol.`

### Root Cause
Selecting `grok-4.7` through Hermes's normal pinned-model path works correctly because that path derives the appropriate protocol. The failure occurs with the plugin's model-only swap. Specifically, in `hermes-jev/__init__.py`, `_on_llm_request` returns a copy of the request with a modified `"model"` field, but does not update the transport/API mode.

---

## Expected Behavior
Routing should not apply a candidate whose required protocol differs from the active connection. If middleware cannot safely switch the transport, it should retain the current model and log an explicit protocol-incompatibility reason.

---

## Impact & Workaround
* **Impact:** Kanban workers failed before completing their tool-driven tasks and were eventually auto-blocked.
* **Workaround:** We turned off routing for the affected profiles while keeping Jev skill selection enabled; workers then proceeded successfully with their configured models.

---

## Suggested Regression Test
1. Set up an active Chat Completions model under OpenCode Go.
2. Include a Responses-only model in the same-provider routing pool.
3. Trigger a routing event that selects the Responses-only model.
4. **Verify:** The plugin keeps the current model (or performs a fully supported transport switch) rather than sending a Responses-only model to `/chat/completions`.

1. Configure OpenCode Go with `glm-5.3-flash`.
2. Add `opencode-go:grok-4.7` to an eligible Jev routing pool and enable routing (`/jev routing on`).
3. Submit a normal turn that triggers Jev to select `grok-4.7` (e.g., via a Kanban worker task).

The captured outgoing request set `model: "grok-4.7"` but was still sent to the Chat Completions endpoint:

title: Expose need_threshold / match_threshold as settings (20-turn sweep: default 0.5/0.5 = 0.64 precision, 0.6/0.6 = 0.78)
body:
**Ask:** make the picker's two gates configurable (`need_threshold`, `match_threshold`). They already exist as kwargs in `jevkit/skillpick.py` but every caller passes literals, so the only way to tune the picker is to patch the kit.

## Why this matters more than it sounds

I ran 20 labelled real turns (production call shape, `top_k=1`, `jev-1.13.0`) against a live homelab agent. Two variables: catalog size, and the gate values.

Catalog 951 skills, shipped 0.5 / 0.5 — 5 correct, 6 wrong, 7 missed, 4 correct silences (precision **0.45**, recall 0.42).

Then I removed the 820-skill security/forensics library from the catalog (it was 85% of the index and 0.4% of actual skill loads) and re-ran the same 20 turns:

| need / match | TP | FP | FN | TN | precision | recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50 / 0.50 (current default) | 7 | 4 | 6 | 4 | 0.64 | 0.54 |
| 0.60 / 0.60 | 7 | 2 | 6 | 6 | **0.78** | 0.54 |

So the catalog change is worth +0.19 precision, and the second gate value is worth another +0.14 — but only the first is reachable from configuration. Latency also fell 1013 ms → 754 ms mean from the same pruning, so the two interact.

## Proposal

- Read both from settings/env (`jev.skills.need_threshold`, `JEV_PICK_NEED_THRESHOLD`, …), same pattern as `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` / `JEV_PROXY_API_KEY`.
- Keep 0.5 / 0.5 as the default so nothing changes for existing users.
- Optionally log the chosen values once at startup, since a stale value in a `.env` is otherwise invisible.

Happy to send the patch with a test that asserts the default is unchanged and that an env override reaches `pick()`, if that is the shape you want.

## Two notes that may affect other reports

- The picker's own benchmark catalog was 379 skills; at 951 the distractors dominate. Anything measured above ~400 skills should probably be read separately.
- `need_threshold` is the field that fails most often in my data: the model says "no skill needed" with 0.58–0.63 confidence on turns that do need one. That is a calibration property of the decision model, not something a higher `match_threshold` can fix.

title: Fix pinned check misreading an Ollama tag for a tagged default
body:
## Problem

With a Hermes `model.default` that carries an Ollama version tag (e.g. `huihui-qwen38-abli:latest`), Jev routing never fired: every turn was treated as an explicit `/model` pin and the default model was used unconditionally. On my installation this produced 237 logged route decisions over ~3 weeks with none of them applied.

## Root cause

```python
default_bare = str(default).split(":", 1)[-1] if default else ""
```

This strip assumes the first colon separates a *provider* prefix from the model id. For an Ollama id the first colon separates the *model name* from its *tag*, so `huihui-qwen38-abli:latest` collapsed to `latest`. The session's full id can never equal `latest`, so `same_default` was permanently `False` and `pinned` permanently `True`.

The existing test suite could not see this because its fixed default (`deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`) contains no colon, where `split(":", 1)[-1]` is a no-op.

## Fix

Strip a provider prefix from the default by exact match (the way `bare` is already normalised one line above), so both sides of the comparison are real Ollama ids. Since an untagged Ollama id means its `latest` tag, both sides are normalised to their effective tag before comparing:

- exact full-id or untagged/`:latest` match on the default core -> unpinned, routing runs
- explicit different tag on the same core -> pinned, the user's `/model` choice wins
- the existing vendor-namespace spelling fallback (custom endpoint reporting a bare id while the default is vendor-qualified) is preserved

## Tests

- `test_tagged_default_model_is_not_treated_as_pinned` — new: tagged default, no `/model`, must route
- `test_explicit_tag_pick_stays_pinned_even_on_the_default_core` — new: same core, different tag, must stay pinned

Full suite: `47/47` in `tests/test_plugin_middleware.py` (45 baseline + 2 new), `146/146` across the plugin test files, `scripts/check_release.py` clean, on main at `8316358`.
